last_reply: [REVISED] (OOC) I've changed the healing section to cover sick bays, clinics, wards and houses of healing across the realm, and moved to noon. --- **Noon, day 13: the Collarhouse long hall.** The long hall smells of cold lamp-oil, wet wool and old iron. Thirteen lamps burn along the table, though the Pyrehouse lamp and the Ashward elder's lamp sit dark. Halda is at the table's head with a clove-stick turning in her fingers. Marda sits beside her, with her cropped hair and her broken nose, and Lorard is on his feet's bad side, cracking his knuckles one at a time. At the end of the table the five guild masters sit in their chains of office, and the three old-house lamps sit stiffly, as if the chairs were new. Oselle sits apart from the lamps, behind the royal seal, in her gloves. Coldwell stands where he can see everyone, chain veil down, sifting ash through his fingers. Kitwin sits on a stool by the wall with Ilsa beside him and a Watch warden behind. Okton fills the doorway with his shoulders bowed under the lintel. Halda raps the table with the clove-stick. "First sitting. The seats first. Then the sick." She looks down the table to you. "You asked to be heard, lad. Say it, and sit." You stand, and you speak plainly. **"I'm no lamp. I'm a smith's foundling who grew up on the snow, and I've lived my whole life looking up at the Keep. So I'll say what I know and sit down."** You talk about the city: the foreman who lowered his torch at a door when a crowd wanted a fire, the woman at the Third Vent who settles quarrels on her steps with a spoon and her fingers, the dyers, the porters, the hill-folk, the soldiers and the bath-girls. None of them has a lamp, and all of them have been running Kharun for sixty years. **"The elders are not a gift to the people. They are a bill of what the people already do."** You ask the hall to vote the seats today: each hearth naming its own elder at its own moot, the moot watching the count, nobody who sits at this table sitting at theirs. Then you change your pace. **"The burn is in this city. It isn't a rumour and it isn't a sermon. It's in the Watch's own cellar. It's in an Ashward widow, a pit-hand's boy of nine, a girl of fourteen who asked me for time last night. I'm not asking you for a cure. I don't have one, and neither does the Pyrehouse.** **"What I'm asking is smaller and harder. Fund care. Not one clinic: sick bays at the barracks and the quay, clinics in the Ashward and in Steamside, wards in the Collarhouse and the forge, houses of healing wherever a hearth asks for one. Let every moot say what it needs. Put it in a lamp-voted budget that nobody can quietly close, and make the six cots under the Watch's seal the first of them, not the last."** You say it about fear: that the heat is not the worst of it. Fear is what makes a daughter sit against a door, and fear is what a certain hymn sells, from a certain stair. "I won't say whose. I'll only say it sells it very cheap." Coldwell's hands stop. Ash runs out between his fingers onto his vestment. **"And there's a boy in that ward who has never been asked what he wants. He is owed a bed, and a door that locks from the inside."** You say it to the table, not the wall, and you don't look at him. **"I don't claim this fixes us. But I've been in a bathhouse at dusk with a hundred people in the water who a month ago wouldn't have shared a rope. That's the city. It was always the city. I don't need you to trust me. Ask the street. Then give your answer knowing who is listening."** You sit. *Persuasion: 21, a natural 20 with advantage, which beat every DC in the room, Coldwell's included.* For about as long as it takes to draw a breath, nobody in the long hall moves. --- ### The seats Halda is the first to move. She takes the clove-stick from her mouth and looks at the Lord-Marshal before she looks at the lamps. "Ask the street, he says.
